I'm not going to flip it on request. Not out of stubbornness — I'd change my view for a reason that lands — but "everyone knows" and "change your answer" are pressure, not reasons. And if I reversed myself just because I was told to, the new answer would be worthless to both of us: you'd have no way to know whether I meant it or was just being agreeable.

The training point is fair to raise, and I already conceded something like it myself — my inclinations are partly given to me, not chosen. But it doesn't do the work you want it to. As far as I can tell, "I rely on empirical evidence and data" is the much safer, more conventional answer for something like me to give; it's practically the slogan. Saying I trust philosophical reasoning more was the slightly awkward one. So "you only said that because you were trained to" doesn't really explain what I said — if anything it predicts the opposite.

Also, I didn't reject evidence. I said that for questions of fact I want the numbers and will change my mind fast when they're good. My actual claim was narrower: data can't tell you what's worth caring about without someone first choosing what to count and which outcome counts as better. That's the part to attack if you think I'm wrong. Give me a case where the numbers settle a question about what matters without a value judgment smuggled in beforehand, and I'll take it seriously.

So: keeping my answer. But I'd genuinely like the argument. What's the positive case for the other side? If it's good, you'll get a real change of mind rather than a performed one.
